newsitem.title: INDIA: Gandhi relative turns to Supreme Court over ashes.
newsitem.headline: Gandhi relative turns to Supreme Court over ashes.

text.p: Mahatma Gandhi's great grandson wants to take the purported ashes of India's apostle of non-violence on a national pilgrimage before immersing them in the Ganges, but he will have to go to the Supreme Court first.

The high court of the eastern state of Orissa said on Sunday that the wooden urn which Tushar Arun Gandhi says contains his great-grandfather's ashes has to be taken directly to the Ganges and not around the country.
Complicating the affair, the state's chief minister says the box does not contain Gandhi's ashes.

"The high court registrar has told me that the urn cannot go around India as I have planned but it has to go directly to Allahabad for immersion," Tushar Arun Gandhi told Reuters in an interview in the eastern city of Bhubaneswar.
After a fast and much media attention, Tushar Arun Gandhi in November won control of the sealed box, which had been in a vault in the State Bank of India in Cuttack town since 1950.
Gandhi was shot dead by a Hindu fanatic on January 30, 1948, five months after India, spurred by Gandhi's campaigning, won independence from Britain. He was cremated in Delhi.
The box, measuring 18 inches by 18 inches by 20 inches (45 cm by 45 cm by 50 cm), bears the inscription "It contains the ashes of Mahatma Gandhi".
But the state's chief minister has called the claims that the box contains Gandhi's ashes "a big hoax".
Gandhi's great grandson planned to take the ashes across the country before immersing them in the Ganges river at Allahabad city on January 30, 49th anniversary of Gandhi's assassination.
The tour would have taken the ashes to sites linked to Gandhi's non-violent campaign against British rule.
The Orissa chief justice said however the ashes would have to be taken straight to northern Allahabad.

There, in a Hindu ceremony which Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda was expected to attend, the ashes were to be immersed at the holy confluence of the Ganges with the Jamuna River and their mythical tributary, the Saraswati River.

"I will now seek clarification from the chief justice of the Supreme Court on this matter," Gandhi's great grandson said. "I think the people of India can't be deprived of their right to see the ashes of the father of the nation."
He said the government of the central state of Madhya Pradesh had offered to fly the ashes to two sites to enable people to pay their respects.
"I am now prepared to walk with the ashes for immersion in the Ganges River. This is a pure sentimental issue," he said.
